card werk-hmr-entry-settles  [open]
The command line's start-up does not wait for the verb, so a hot reload can run
why: Bun's hot reload waits until the program's first evaluation ends. The serve verb runs until the server stops. A start-up that waited for its verb would never end under serve, so no edit would ever reload.

The start-up of the command line loads the verbs and starts the chosen verb. It does not wait for the verb's result as part of its own evaluation. When the verb ends, a callback exits with the verb's exit code. So the first evaluation ends at once, and a later edit of any module reloads it in the same process (see #werk-hmr for the runtime and the guard).

Example:

- The server runs under hot reload. The chat child C runs a turn.

1. The start-up loads the verbs, starts the serve verb, and ends.
2. An agent saves an edit to a server module. Bun evaluates the modules again.
3. The serve verb finds the live server on the global object and swaps in the new request handler. C keeps its turn.
4. The person stops the server. The serve verb ends, and the callback exits with its code.

If the start-up waited for the verb, nothing would reload in step 2. The reload waits for an evaluation that never ends.

```
start-up:  load verbs -> start serve -> end      (no wait on serve)
edit:      evaluate again -> swap handler        (C keeps its turn)
stop:      serve ends -> callback -> exit with serve's code
```

  -> depends_on      werk-hmr-swap  A hot reload keeps the server and swaps in the new request handler
       why: takes the reload that evaluates the start-up again and swaps the handler, which this rule lets start
  -> refines         werk-hmr  Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
  -> depends_on      werk-verb-registry  Each command-line verb lives in its own module and registers itself, so a new verb edits no shared list
       why: takes the verbs that register themselves, which the start-up loads before it starts one
